setSeclabChannelGuard.why: patch 0006: whoever calls the setter last decides the channel guard for the whole process. The workbench installs the real guard (seclabRpcFilter.ts, patch 0005); the REH, which runs inside the tab, installs an allow-all as the first statement of createServer. A third caller reachable from desktop could replace the workbench guard and silently reopen every chan: surface, and reach.json/unreachable.json would not notice.

AgentHostIpcChannels.RemoteProxy.why: patch 0015 gates the agent-host transport by wrapping this channel inside EditorRemoteAgentHostServiceClient, so every caller that instantiates that client is gated (including patch 0010's selection in agentHostService.ts). A second renderer-side consumer would bypass the gate entirely, and no runtime probe can show that none exists.

ExtHostContext.ExtHostDocumentsAndEditor.why: patch 0035 filters which text models reach a tab extension host inside MainThreadDocumentsAndEditors. A second window-side holder of this proxy could push host documents past the filter, and no runtime probe can show that none exists.

ExtHostContext.ExtHostDocuments).why: patch 0035: model content changes and dirty, save and encoding events reach a tab only through MainThreadDocuments, whose ModelTracker and file events apply the same provenance filter. A second window-side getProxy of this shape would bypass it.

__upstreamInvariants.why: facts about upstream that a patch's security argument depends on, which no unit test can hold because the unit container has no upstream checkout. Checked over the patched tree by build/check-sole-consumer.ts, which patch-build already runs.

rules.why: patch 0017 pins workbench.browser.dataStorage to 'ephemeral' precisely because upstream drops the browser view's network for the global scope and keeps it for ephemeral. If either branch changes, the pinned value must be re-derived before it can still be trusted.

rules.why: the browser TOOL supplies its own session scope, so `workbench.browser.dataStorage` is never consulted on the agent-tool path at all: `_resolveSessionRequest` returns a request verbatim when it already carries a scope. The U-vs-F proof therefore measures that key on the non-agent create path (a restored editor, a user-opened view), and no claim about the browser tool may be drawn from it. Recorded because this is the whole reason the dataStorage half is pinned by source reading rather than by the tool probe (security review rounds 8 and 9, finding `the dataStorage half is never exercised`). If upstream stops supplying a scope here, the tool path starts reading the setting and the probe's scope becomes the stronger evidence -- a change we must notice.

the early return is what makes the invariant above load-bearing: a session request that already carries a scope is returned verbatim, WITHOUT reading `workbench.browser.dataStorage`. Patch 0017 also relies on the configured-storage branch still existing and still reading that exact setting id, since the patch fixes the value the window reads there. If either half changes, the 0017 security argument and the increment 2 proof both need rereading.

patch 0018 decides which chat sessions a tab window may address by comparing the connection OBJECT that `resolveSessionResource` returns with `ambientConnection`. That comparison is only meaningful because upstream returns the same injected `IAgentHostService` from both: `ambientConnection` returns it directly, and `getConnectionByAuthority` returns it for the ambient authority, which is what `resolveSessionResource` goes through. If upstream ever wrapped or copied either side, reference equality would stop holding and 0018 would refuse this window's own agent-host session -- failing closed, but silently breaking the agent host rather than reporting it. Pinned so that change fails the patch build instead.

patch 0018 refuses a chat request unless the session resolves to THIS window's own agent-host connection AND `backendSessionIsAdvertised` is true. Both halves are needed because of these two lines together: `resolveSessionResourceIdentity` does not fail on an unknown session, it SYNTHESISES an ambient identity from any `agent-host-*` scheme, and `getConnectionByAuthority(AMBIENT_AGENT_HOST_AUTHORITY)` then returns the same object as `ambientConnection`. So a connection-identity check alone would have been a scheme-prefix string test one layer down, which is the very thing the patch exists to avoid. `backendSessionIsAdvertised` is the only signal that separates a registry hit from the synthesised fallback. If upstream makes the fallback fail, or sets the flag anywhere but on a `_backendSessions` hit, the patch's argument must be re-derived.

patch 0018 reads `backendSessionIsAdvertised` off the session RESOLUTION, but upstream only ever sets that flag on the IDENTITY, in `_createSessionIdentity`. It reaches the resolution solely through this spread. If upstream built the resolution field by field instead, the flag would silently become undefined and the gate would deny every request: fail-closed, but silently, which is the failure mode the gate's verdict logging exists to prevent (security review round 2, alert 4).

patches 0015 and 0018 both decide whether agents are on from `inspect().policyValue` and `.defaultValue` only, never `getValue()`, because a tab extension can write the user, workspace and remote layers. That leaves `defaultValue` as the one remaining route, reachable through an extension's `configurationDefaults` contribution. It is closed because `seclab.agents.enabled` is registered at ConfigurationScope.APPLICATION and these lines reject a default override for any scope outside the allowed set. If the allowed scopes grow to include APPLICATION, or the scope check is dropped, a tab extension could turn agents on and the enablement rule must be re-derived (security review round 2, alert 4).
